lessons.title: The ethics and principles of permaculture
lessons.html:
What is permaculture?

Permaculture is a design approach for productive land use that copies the patterns of natural ecosystems. The word comes from "permanent agriculture". It was developed in Australia in the 1970s by Bill Mollison and David Holmgren and is widely used in South African food gardens, smallholdings and community projects.

The three ethics

  • Earth care: look after soil, water, forests and biodiversity.
  • People care: meet people's needs for food, shelter, work and community.
  • Fair share: limit consumption and return surplus to earth and people.

Core design principles

Different authors list the principles differently, but these ideas are common:

  1. Observe and interact: spend time watching sun, wind, water flow, soils and wildlife on the site before changing it.
  2. Catch and store energy: harvest rainwater, store water in soil, use sun and biomass.
  3. Obtain a yield: the system must produce food, fuel, fodder or income.
  4. Produce no waste: every output becomes an input, e.g. kitchen waste to compost, manure to beds.
  5. Integrate rather than segregate: place elements so they help each other, e.g. chickens near the orchard to eat pests and add manure.
  6. Use small and slow solutions: start small, learn, then expand.
  7. Use and value diversity: many species reduce risk from pests, disease and weather.
  8. Use edges: boundaries between systems, such as a pond edge, are highly productive.
  9. Each element performs many functions; each function is supported by many elements.

Why it matters in South Africa

With erratic rainfall, degraded soils and high input costs, permaculture offers low-cost ways to grow food: water harvesting, mulching, composting and diverse planting reduce dependence on bought fertiliser, chemicals and water.

lessons.title: Applying the principles in practice
lessons.html:
Zones

Permaculture places elements by how often they need attention:

ZoneUse
0The house or work centre
1Daily-use herbs, salad greens, seedlings, compost
2Fruit trees, larger vegetable beds, poultry
3Main crops, field crops, larger livestock
4Woodlots, fodder, semi-managed grazing
5Wild, natural area left for observation and biodiversity

Sectors

Sectors are energies coming from outside: sun angle in summer and winter, prevailing wind, fire risk, water flow, views and noise. Place windbreaks against hot, dry winds, firebreaks on the fire-risk side and shade-tolerant crops on the shady side.

Practical techniques

  • Swales: ditches dug on contour with a mound below, to slow and sink rainwater.
  • Mulching: cover soil with straw, leaves or grass to reduce evaporation and feed soil life.
  • Composting and worm farms: turn waste into fertility.
  • Guilds and companion planting: e.g. maize, beans and pumpkin grown together.
  • Food forests: layered planting of trees, shrubs, herbs and groundcovers.
  • Greywater use: reuse lightly used household water on non-edible plants or trees, following local rules.
  • Integrated animals: chicken tractors to clear and fertilise beds.

Applying observation

Before digging, observe through a season if possible. Mark where water ponds after rain, where frost lies, and which areas get afternoon sun. Map existing trees and soil types. Then design.

Safety

Digging swales and ponds needs care: watch for buried pipes and cables, keep slopes stable, and fence ponds where children are present. Use tools correctly and wear gloves and boots.

Key points

  • Permaculture rests on earth care, people care and fair share.
  • Observe the site before designing.
  • Zones place elements by how often they are used.
  • Sectors guide placement against wind, sun, fire and water.
  • Techniques include swales, mulch, compost, guilds and integrated animals.
